data.name: CI/CD Pipeline (GitHub Actions)
data.description: 17 GitHub Actions workflows (.github/workflows/) covering CI testing, CodeQL analysis, release packaging, container image publishing, ZAP security scanning, dependency update automation (Dependabot), and stale issue management. Workflows use npm ci for installs and produce Docker container images. Several workflows lack explicit permissions blocks and use unpinned actions (SHA pinning absent).

threats.title: [F-025] Remote Script Execution via Unverified Installer (ci.yml:358)
threats.description:
At ci.yml:358, the heroku job downloads and immediately pipes the Heroku CLI installer to sh without checksum or signature verification: `curl https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh | sh`. An attacker who compromises the Heroku CDN, performs DNS hijacking, or stages a MITM against the TLS connection can serve a modified installer executing arbitrary code in the GitHub Actions runner. The heroku job lacks an explicit permissions block, so GITHUB_TOKEN may carry write-level access to repository contents, packages, and Releases. The job also mounts the HEROKU_API_KEY secret, so a malicious script could exfiltrate both credentials in a single execution. The job is gated on `github.repository == 'juice-shop/juice-shop'` which limits fork exposure but does not protect against upstream CDN compromise.

Impact: Arbitrary code execution in CI with access to GITHUB_TOKEN and Heroku API key, enabling repository takeover or deployment of malicious release artifacts.

Risk: High (likelihood Low, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-829
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml:358 contains `curl https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh | sh` with no integrity check.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:358

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-025 (F-025)
threats.mitigation:
M-024 — Pin third-party dependencies to immutable versions (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Remove the `curl https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh | sh` step from .github/workflows/ci.yml:358.
2. Replace it with the official `akhileshns/heroku-deploy` action already used at line 369 (it bundles the CLI internally), or download a version-pinned Heroku CLI tarball and verify its SHA-256 checksum before executing.
3. Add an explicit `permissions: contents: read` block to the heroku job to limit blast radius if any step is compromised.
Verification: Trigger the heroku workflow and confirm: (1) the `curl | sh` pattern is absent from runner logs; (2) the SHA-256 check step exits 0; (3) a wrong checksum causes the job to fail before any CLI execution.
Reference: CWE-829

threats.title: [F-026] Unpinned GitHub Actions Allow Supply Chain Code Injection
threats.description:
Seven GitHub Actions use mutable version references instead of commit-SHA pins. The highest-risk case is `calibreapp/image-actions@main` in image_actions.yml: a floating main branch allows any push to the upstream default branch to immediately alter code running in the next CI trigger without review. `coverallsapp/github-action@v2` at ci.yml:188 runs with GITHUB_TOKEN and uploads test coverage data. The three `github/codeql-action/*@v3` entries hold `security-events: write` permission. For any of these, an upstream repository compromise — stolen maintainer credential, rogue collaborator, or upstream CI hijack — immediately results in malicious code executing under the repository's GITHUB_TOKEN. Additionally, Dockerfile:1 references `node:24` and Dockerfile:22 references `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13` without digest pins, making production container builds non-reproducible and vulnerable to silent base-image substitution.

Impact: Upstream compromise results in arbitrary code execution in CI with GITHUB_TOKEN write access, enabling repository content modification, secret exfiltration, or publication of backdoored container images.

Risk: High (likelihood Low, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-1104
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml:188 uses `coverallsapp/github-action@v2` (floating tag); image_actions.yml uses `calibreapp/image-actions@main` (floating branch); Dockerfile:1 and Dockerfile:22 reference base images without digest pins.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:188

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-026 (F-026)
threats.mitigation:
M-025 — Pin the container base image to an immutable digest (priority P2, effort Low)
1. For each unpinned action, resolve the full commit SHA for the current tag via `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/git/ref/tags/<tag>` and replace the floating ref with the SHA plus a comment, e.g. `calibreapp/image-actions@<sha> # main@<date>`.
2. For Dockerfile:1, change `FROM node:24` to `FROM node:24@sha256:<digest>`. Retrieve the digest with `docker pull node:24 && docker inspect node:24 --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'`.
3. For Dockerfile:22, add `@sha256:<digest>` to the gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13 reference.
4. Extend the existing Dependabot configuration in .github/dependabot.yml to cover `package-ecosystem: github-actions` so future version bumps arrive as PRs rather than silent tag moves.
5. Enable CODEOWNERS enforcement on workflow files so changes to .github/workflows/ require maintainer review.
Verification: Run `grep -rn '@main\|@v[0-9]' .github/workflows/` and confirm zero results. Run `grep -E '^FROM [^@]+$' Dockerfile` and confirm zero unpinned FROM lines.
Reference: CWE-1104

threats.title: [F-044] Excessive GITHUB_TOKEN Scope from Missing Permissions Blocks in 11 Workflows
threats.description:
Eleven GitHub Actions workflows lack an explicit `permissions:` block at the workflow or job level. When no permissions block is declared, the GITHUB_TOKEN inherits the repository's default permission policy. If the repository uses GitHub's default of read-and-write permissions, every workflow without a declared permissions block operates with broad write access to contents, packages, deployments, issues, pull-requests, and other scopes. A successful compromise of any of these 11 workflows — via a malicious unpinned action (ci-cd-pipeline-002) or the Heroku curl installer (ci-cd-pipeline-001) — immediately grants full repository write access without requiring any additional privilege escalation. Only codeql-analysis.yml, pr-compliance.yml, and lock.yml declare explicit permissions blocks; ci.yml, image_actions.yml, release.yml, and 8 others carry none.

Impact: A CI runner compromise in any of the 11 unscoped workflows escalates directly to full repository write access — commit forgery, release artifact tampering, package publication — without additional privilege exploitation.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-284
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
grep for `permissions:` across .github/workflows/ returns only 3 of 14 workflow files; ci.yml, image_actions.yml, release.yml, and 8 others carry no explicit permissions block.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:1

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-044 (F-044)
threats.mitigation:
M-043 — Apply least-privilege filesystem access (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Set the repository default to read-only: Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions → select 'Read repository contents and packages'.
2. Add an explicit `permissions:` block at the top of each of the 11 workflows. Use `permissions: contents: read` as the safe baseline for test workflows, then grant only the scopes the workflow actually uses.
3. For release.yml (publishes packages and containers), scope to `contents: write, packages: write` only.
4. For ci.yml's heroku job, use `permissions: contents: read` since it only deploys and does not write to the repository.
5. Verify with `grep -rL 'permissions:' .github/workflows/*.yml` after the change; expected output is empty.

data.name: Authentication & Session Surface
data.description: Login, token/session issuance, password-reset and MFA handlers (lib/insecurity.ts, lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts, routes/2fa.ts, routes/authenticatedUsers.ts, …). The credential-bearing entry surface — the highest-value authentication boundary in the system.

threats.title: [F-002] Missing Security Audit Logging Across Components
threats.description:
None of the authentication route handlers — `routes/login.ts`, `routes/2fa.ts`, `routes/resetPassword.ts` — emit a structured security event when authentication succeeds or fails, when a 2FA challenge is attempted, or when a password reset is completed. An attacker who successfully authenticates via SQL injection (`auth-001`) or forges a JWT (`auth-002`) leaves no record in any log. Incident response teams investigating a breach cannot determine when admin credentials were first abused, which accounts were accessed, or how many failed attempts preceded a successful compromise. This absence also prevents anomaly detection (e.g., alerting on repeated failed logins for one account).

Impact: Successful authentication attacks are invisible — no forensic reconstruction of the breach timeline is possible after the fact.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-778
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
No call to a security logger or audit sink appears in `routes/login.ts`, `routes/2fa.ts`, or `routes/resetPassword.ts`; authentication outcomes (success, failure, IP, userId) are not recorded.
- routes/login.ts:48

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-002 (F-002)
threats.mitigation:
M-002 — Add security audit logging (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Add a security logger (e.g., `winston` with a dedicated transport) that records at minimum: `timestamp`, `event_type` (login_success, login_failure, 2fa_success, 2fa_failure, password_reset), `userId` or `email`, `ip`, `user_agent`.
2. In `routes/login.ts`, log inside both the success path (`afterLogin`) and the `else if (!user.data?.id)` failure branch at line 50.
3. In `routes/resetPassword.ts`, log on success at line 43 and on wrong-answer failure at line 49.
4. Route the security log to an append-only sink (separate file, SIEM, or remote log service) distinct from the application debug log.
Verification: Perform a successful login followed by a failed login; assert the security log contains two events with the correct `event_type` values and no sensitive fields (password, token).
Reference: CWE-778

threats.title: [F-004] SQL Injection on Login (routes/login.ts:34)
threats.description:
An attacker submits `' OR '1'='1'--` as the email field on `POST /rest/user/login`. Because `req.body.email` flows unescaped into `models.sequelize.query()` at `routes/login.ts:34`, the payload short-circuits the WHERE clause and returns the first user row in the `Users` table — the seeded admin account. The server calls `afterLogin()`, mints a valid RS256 JWT bearing the admin identity, and returns it in the response. The attacker gains full admin access without knowing any credential.

Impact: Unauthenticated attacker gains a valid admin JWT, bypassing all access controls on every privileged endpoint.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-89
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`routes/login.ts:34` builds the login query by string-concatenating `req.body.email` and `security.hash(req.body.password)` into a raw `models.sequelize.query()` call instead of using Sequelize parameterised binding.
- routes/login.ts:34

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-2 external → auth (internet-facing): SQL injection short-circuits the credential match at routes/login.ts:34, so a JWT is issued without any valid password — breaking the tb-2 assumption that a JWT is only issued after credential verification.
- tb-5 backend-api → data-store-sqlite (internal): routes/login.ts:34 uses raw string interpolation in models.sequelize.query() instead of parameterized Sequelize model methods, breaking the tb-5 assumption of parameterized binding.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-004 (F-004)
threats.mitigation:
M-004 — Use parameterized database queries (priority P1, effort Low)
1. Replace `models.sequelize.query(...)` at `routes/login.ts:34` with `UserModel.findOne({ where: { email: req.body.email, password: security.hash(req.body.password), deletedAt: null } })` using Sequelize ORM methods.
2. Remove the raw SQL string template entirely; Sequelize's `where` clause uses parameterized binding by default.
3. Add an integration test that submits `' OR '1'='1'--` as the email and asserts HTTP 401 is returned.
4. Replace the raw `sequelize.query()` call at routes/login.ts:34 with `UserModel.findOne({ where: { email: req.body.email, password: security.hash(req.body.password), deletedAt: null } })`.
5. Upgrade the password hashing algorithm from MD5 to bcrypt or Argon2 (see backend-api-014) — this is a pre-requisite for treating the password field as a proper credential.
6. Add express-rate-limit middleware to POST /rest/user/login (see backend-api-016).
Verification: Submit `POST /rest/user/login` with `{"email":"' OR '1'='1'--","password":"x"}` and assert the response is HTTP 401, not a JWT-bearing 200.
Reference: CWE-89

threats.title: [F-005] Hardcoded RSA Private Key (lib/insecurity.ts:21)
threats.description:
The RSA private key used to sign every JWT in the application is committed verbatim as a PEM string literal at `lib/insecurity.ts:21`. Anyone who reads the public repository can extract this key and call `jwt.sign({ data: { email: 'admin@juice-sh.op', role: 'admin' } }, privateKey, { algorithm: 'RS256', expiresIn: '6h' })` to produce a token that `security.isAuthorized()` and `jws.verify()` at `lib/insecurity.ts:52-55` accept as valid. The attacker can forge a token for any email address, any role, and any privilege level without interacting with the login endpoint.

Impact: Any reader of the public repository can forge a valid JWT for any identity or role, permanently compromising the entire JWT trust model.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-321
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: configuration-defect

Evidence:
`lib/insecurity.ts:21` hardcodes the RSA private key as a string literal; `lib/insecurity.ts:54` uses this same key in `jwt.sign()` for every session token.
- lib/insecurity.ts:21

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-2 external → auth (internet-facing): With the private key publicly available, an attacker can forge a JWT for any identity without going through credential verification, breaking the tb-2 assumption that tokens are only issued after credential match.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-005 (F-005)
threats.mitigation:
M-005 — Move cryptographic keys to a managed secret store (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Remove the hardcoded private key string from `lib/insecurity.ts:21` and replace with `process.env.JWT_PRIVATE_KEY` (or a secret manager call); fail startup when the variable is absent.
2. Generate a new RSA-2048 or EC P-256 key pair and treat the old key as permanently compromised — invalidate all existing sessions.
3. Store the public key path or value in a separate non-secret config entry; verify it is served for token validation.
4. Add a CI check (e.g., `truffleHog` or `gitleaks`) that rejects commits containing PEM key patterns.
Verification: Run `grep -r 'BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY' lib/` and assert zero hits; then verify a JWT signed with the old key is rejected with HTTP 401.
Reference: CWE-321

threats.title: [F-014] Security Question-Only Password Reset (routes/resetPassword.ts:35)
threats.description:
The `POST /rest/user/reset-password` handler accepts `email`, `answer`, and `newPassword`. At `routes/resetPassword.ts:35-41`, it looks up the `SecurityAnswer` row for the provided email and compares `security.hmac(answer)` to the stored HMAC. No secondary channel (email link, SMS code) is used; knowing or guessing the security question answer is sufficient to reset any account's password. Security question answers (mother's maiden name, pet name, favourite colour) are commonly guessable from social media or public records. The admin account's security question and its answer are discoverable via OSINT because they correspond to fictional characters refe**** (10 chars) in the application's public GitHub repository.

Impact: An attacker who can research or guess a security question answer can reset any user's password and immediately take over that account.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-640
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`routes/resetPassword.ts:35` looks up the `SecurityAnswer` model record by email and at line 41 compares `security.hmac(answer)` to the stored value — a correct answer alone triggers `user.update({ password: newPassword })` with no email confirmation or second-factor verification.
- routes/resetPassword.ts:35

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-014 (F-014)
threats.mitigation:
M-013 — Replace security-question reset with email-verified one-time reset link (priority P2, effort High)
1. Replace the security-question reset flow with a time-limited, single-use reset token delivered to the account's verified email address.
2. Generate a cryptographically random token (≥32 bytes, using `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')`), store its SHA-256 hash in the DB with a 15-minute expiry, and email the raw token to the user.
3. The `POST /rest/user/reset-password` endpoint accepts only the raw token; reject it after first use and after expiry.
4. Until the security-question flow is replaced, additionally require email confirmation before applying the password change.
Verification: Attempt to reset an account's password using a known security answer and assert the endpoint returns HTTP 403; verify the reset only succeeds after clicking the link sent to the registered email.
Reference: CWE-640

threats.title: [F-029] Weak Password Hash MD5 without Salt (lib/insecurity.ts:41)
threats.description:
All passwords are hashed with unsalted MD5 at `lib/insecurity.ts:41` before storage in the `Users` table. MD5 is a cryptographic hash with no work factor and no per-user salt, so a database dump (obtainable via the SQL injection at `routes/login.ts:34` or a direct DB breach) immediately yields crackable hashes. An attacker who runs the dump against a standard MD5 rainbow table or a GPU-accelerated cracker (e.g., `hashcat -m 0`) recovers all plaintext passwords in minutes. Since users commonly reuse passwords, this breach extends to external services.

Impact: A database breach (or SQL injection) exposes all user passwords as effectively plaintext — MD5 rainbow tables for common passwords are publicly available.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-916
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
`lib/insecurity.ts:41` exports `hash = (data: string) => crypto.createHash('md5').update(data).digest('hex')` — this single-round, unsalted MD5 call is used as the application's sole password hashing primitive.
- lib/insecurity.ts:41

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-029 (F-029)
threats.mitigation:
M-028 — Hash passwords with a strong, salted algorithm (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Replace `crypto.createHash('md5')` in `lib/insecurity.ts:41` with `bcrypt.hash(password, 12)` (using the `bcryptjs` or `bcrypt` npm package) which includes a per-call salt.
2. Add a `UserModel` `beforeCreate` / `beforeUpdate` hook that calls `bcrypt.hash()` automatically, removing the need for callers to invoke `security.hash()` directly.
3. On first login with the new code, detect MD5-format hashes (32 hex chars) and re-hash the verified plaintext; retire the MD5 path once all users have migrated.
4. Update the login query at `routes/login.ts:34` to use `bcrypt.compare(password, user.password)` instead of hash-in-SQL.
Verification: Register a user and verify the stored password column is a bcrypt hash (starts with `$2b$`); verify login with the correct password succeeds and with a wrong password returns HTTP 401.
Reference: CWE-916

threats.title: [F-038] Missing Login Rate Limiting (routes/login.ts)
threats.description:
The `POST /rest/user/login` handler in `routes/login.ts` carries no rate-limiting middleware. An attacker can issue thousands of login requests per second with different passwords against a known email address — or use a credential-stuffing list — without triggering any throttle, lockout, or CAPTCHA. Because passwords are MD5-hashed (CWE-916, `lib/insecurity.ts:41`), an offline brute-force of the hash requires only rainbow-table lookups; but an online attack against `/rest/user/login` is equally viable since there is no per-IP or per-account request limit.

Impact: An attacker can brute-force or credential-stuff any user account without detection or throttling, making account takeover a matter of connection speed.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-307
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`routes/login.ts` has no call to `rateLimit`, `slowDown`, or equivalent middleware before the `models.sequelize.query()` call that validates credentials.
- routes/login.ts:32

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-038 (F-038)
threats.mitigation:
M-037 — Rate-limit and lock out repeated authentication attempts (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Install `express-rate-limit` and apply a limiter of 10 requests per 15 minutes per IP address on `POST /rest/user/login` in `server.ts` before the route handler.
2. Add a second per-account limiter keyed on `req.body.email` to prevent distributed attacks from multiple IPs against one account.
3. On repeated failures (≥5), return HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header; log the throttled account and IP for alerting.
4. Add a test that sends 11 login requests in rapid succession and asserts the 11th returns HTTP 429.
Verification: Replay 11 `POST /rest/user/login` requests within 1 minute from the same IP and assert the 11th response is HTTP 429.
Reference: CWE-307

threats.title: [F-042] Deluxe Tier Token Derivable from Committed Private Key (lib/insecurity.ts:150)
threats.description:
The `deluxeToken()` function at `lib/insecurity.ts:149-152` computes `HMAC-SHA256(email + 'deluxe', privateKey)` using the same RSA private key string committed at line 21. The `isDeluxe()` check at line 167 accepts a JWT with `role: 'deluxe'` only when the JWT's `deluxeToken` claim equals `deluxeToken(email)`. Because the private key is publicly committed to the repository, an attacker can: (1) compute a valid `deluxeToken` for their own email using the known key, (2) craft a JWT with `role: 'deluxe'` and the computed `deluxeToken`, signed with the private key. The `isDeluxe()` check passes, granting deluxe-tier privileges (e.g., reduced prices, exclusive product access) for any account.

Impact: Any attacker with the public source repository can generate a valid deluxe-tier JWT for their account, gaining deluxe-tier pricing and access without a subscription.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-321
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`lib/insecurity.ts:150` calls `crypto.createHmac('sha256', privateKey)` where `privateKey` is the publicly committed literal from line 21; the result of `deluxeToken(email)` is checkable offline by any reader of the source.
- lib/insecurity.ts:150

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-042 (F-042)
threats.mitigation:
M-041 — Move cryptographic keys to a managed secret store (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Remove the hardcoded `privateKey` (covered in auth-002 remediation) — rotating the key also invalidates all existing `deluxeToken` values.
2. Store the deluxe-token derivation secret separately from the JWT signing key in `process.env.DELUXE_TOKEN_SECRET`.
3. Replace the `deluxeToken(email)` computation with a server-side lookup in the `Orders` or `DeluxeSubscriptions` table, removing the need for a client-verifiable HMAC at all.
Verification: Using the old private key, compute a deluxe token and include it in a forged JWT; assert the `isDeluxe()` check returns false after the key is rotated.
Reference: CWE-321

threats.title: [F-049] Trusted X-User-Email Header without Authentication (lib/insecurity.ts:93)
threats.description:
The exported function `userEmailFrom()` at `lib/insecurity.ts:93` reads `headers['x-user-email']` from the incoming request and returns it as the user's email identity, with no validation that the header matches the authenticated JWT's email claim. Any request reaching a handler that calls `userEmailFrom()` for identity decisions can supply an arbitrary email address in `X-User-Email` to impersonate other users, including the admin account. This is an HTTP-header spoofing primitive: because the header is an attacker-controlled string, it bypasses any credential check that a legitimate JWT would otherwise enforce.

Impact: Any authenticated (or unauthenticated) caller can inject an arbitrary X-User-Email header to impersonate another user in endpoints that rely on `userEmailFrom()` for identity.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-290
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`lib/insecurity.ts:93` exports `userEmailFrom({ headers }) => headers['x-user-email']` with no JWT cross-reference; callers receive the raw header value as the user's email identity.
- lib/insecurity.ts:93

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-049 (F-049)
threats.mitigation:
M-048 — Derive user email exclusively from the verified JWT claim, not from request hea… (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Replace calls to `userEmailFrom(req)` with `security.authenticatedUsers.from(req)?.data?.email` to read the email from the server-side in-memory token map, which can only be populated via successful JWT verification.
2. Remove or deprecate the `userEmailFrom` export to prevent future misuse.
3. Add a test that submits a request with `X-User-Email: admin@juice-sh.op` while authenticated as a regular user and asserts the handler uses the JWT's email, not the header.
Verification: Send a request with `X-User-Email: admin@juice-sh.op` to any handler that calls `userEmailFrom()` while authenticated as a non-admin user and confirm the response treats the caller as the non-admin JWT identity.
Reference: CWE-290

threats.title: [F-052] IP Address Spoofing via True-Client-IP Header (routes/saveLoginIp.ts:18)
threats.description:
After a successful login, the handler at `routes/saveLoginIp.ts:18` stores `req.headers['true-client-ip']` directly as the user's `lastLoginIp` in the `Users` table. No proxy whitelist or validation is applied — any HTTP client can include `True-Client-IP: <arbitrary string>` and have it written to the database. An attacker can set this header to an arbitrary value (e.g., a colleague's office IP, `127.0.0.1`, or an XSS payload) to corrupt the stored login origin. This tampers with the audit record used for forensic investigation of account compromise and can be used to frame other users.

Impact: The IP address in the `lastLoginIp` column is untrustworthy, undermining forensic analysis of login events and enabling an attacker to plant false attribution data.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Low)
CWE: CWE-290
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`routes/saveLoginIp.ts:18` reads `req.headers['true-client-ip']` without validating that the request arrived via a trusted proxy; the raw header value is passed to `user.update({ lastLoginIp: ... })` at line 32.
- routes/saveLoginIp.ts:18

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-052 (F-052)
threats.mitigation:
M-051 — Accept True-Client-IP only when the request originates from a trusted reverse p… (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Replace the unconditional `req.headers['true-client-ip']` read with a check that only trusts the header when the request source (`req.socket.remoteAddress`) matches a configured trusted-proxy CIDR allowlist.
2. Fall back to `utils.toSimpleIpAddress(req.socket.remoteAddress)` for all other requests.
3. Apply the same pattern to any other forwarding headers (`X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Real-IP`) consumed elsewhere in the codebase.
Verification: Send a login request with `True-Client-IP: 1.2.3.4` from an untrusted source and verify `lastLoginIp` in the database reflects the actual socket address, not `1.2.3.4`.
Reference: CWE-290

threats.title: [F-056] Hardcoded HMAC Key for Security Answer Storage (lib/insecurity.ts:42)
threats.description:
The `hmac()` function at `lib/insecurity.ts:42` uses the hardcoded key `'pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj'` as the HMAC-SHA256 secret for all security answers. Because this key is in the public source repository, any attacker can precompute the HMAC of candidate answers offline: `crypto.createHmac('sha256', 'pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj').update('Samuel').digest('hex')`. Comparing the output against the `SecurityAnswer` table (obtainable via SQLi) reveals whether a given answer matches — turning the HMAC into an effective lookup table. This removes the main purpose of HMAC as a keyed primitive: without key secrecy, it reduces to a simple hash.

Impact: An attacker with a copy of the SecurityAnswer table can verify any candidate answer offline without submitting to the rate-limited reset endpoint.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-321
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: configuration-defect

Evidence:
`lib/insecurity.ts:42` hardcodes `'pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj'` as the HMAC-SHA256 key; this same function is called at `routes/resetPassword.ts:41` to compare submitted answers to the stored HMAC.
- lib/insecurity.ts:42

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-056 (F-056)
threats.mitigation:
M-055 — Move cryptographic keys to a managed secret store (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Replace `'pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj'` in `lib/insecurity.ts:42` with `process.env.HMAC_SECRET`; fail startup when absent.
2. Preferably, replace HMAC entirely with `bcrypt.hash(answer, 12)` for security answers — bcrypt's work factor makes offline dictionary attacks expensive even if the key is leaked.
3. Rotate all stored security answer HMACs on next user interaction by re-hashing on first successful answer comparison.
Verification: Verify the HMAC_SECRET environment variable is required at startup (`unset HMAC_SECRET && node server.js` should exit non-zero); confirm `grep pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj lib/insecurity.ts` returns no output.
Reference: CWE-321

threats.title: [F-057] MFA Intermediate Token Returned for Client-Side Storage (routes/login.ts:41)
threats.description:
When a user with 2FA enabled completes the password step, `routes/login.ts:38-44` returns HTTP 401 with body `{ status: 'totp_token_required', data: { tmpToken: <signed JWT> } }`. The frontend stores this `tmpToken` in `localStorage` during the 2FA challenge step (per CONTROLS: 'TOTP temp token stored in localStorage during challenge step'). Any XSS payload executed in the browser during this window can read the token from `localStorage` and present it to `POST /rest/2fa/verify` paired with a brute-forced TOTP code (see auth-011). The design couples two weaknesses: client-side storage of a server-issued token and no rate limit on verification.

Impact: An XSS payload executing during the 2FA challenge window can steal the intermediate token and use it to complete the 2FA challenge, bypassing the second factor.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-522
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`routes/login.ts:41` returns the `tmpToken` as a signed JWT in the HTTP response body for the client to store; the CONTROLS section confirms it is stored in `localStorage`, where JavaScript can read it.
- routes/login.ts:41

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-057 (F-057)
threats.mitigation:
M-056 — Store the 2FA intermediate token in an HttpOnly session cookie, not localStorage (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Replace the `tmpToken` in the JSON response body with a server-side session identifier (e.g., a signed `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie) that maps to the pending 2FA state.
2. The `POST /rest/2fa/verify` endpoint reads the pending state from the server-side session, not from a client-supplied token.
3. As an interim measure, shorten the tmpToken lifetime to 2 minutes (instead of the default 6 hours inherited from `security.authorize()`) to limit the attack window.
Verification: Complete the password step and inspect browser localStorage; assert no JWT-shaped value is stored after the 2FA prompt appears.
Reference: CWE-522

threats.title: [F-062] Missing Rate Limiting on 2FA Verification Endpoint (routes/2fa.ts:16)
threats.description:
The `verify()` handler at `routes/2fa.ts:16` accepts a `tmpToken` (the intermediate 2FA challenge token issued after successful password entry) and a `totpToken` (6-digit TOTP code). There is no rate limiting on this endpoint. A TOTP code is 6 decimal digits (10^6 possibilities). With a 30-second validity window and the `epochTolerance: 30` parameter at `routes/2fa.ts:31` accepting codes one window before and after, an attacker who obtains a valid `tmpToken` (e.g., via phishing or MITM) can automate 1,000,000 requests to brute-force the TOTP token within the validity window — bypassing the 2FA second factor entirely.

Impact: An attacker who intercepts or phishes the `tmpToken` can brute-force the 6-digit TOTP code and complete 2FA authentication without the victim's authenticator app.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-307
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`routes/2fa.ts:16` defines the `verify` handler with no `rateLimit` middleware call; the `totpToken` field is validated only for correctness, not for attempt frequency.
- routes/2fa.ts:16

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-062 (F-062)
threats.mitigation:
M-061 — Rate-limit and lock out repeated authentication attempts (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Apply `express-rate-limit` on `POST /rest/2fa/verify` with a limit of 5 attempts per 5-minute window per IP and per `tmpToken` claim.
2. After 5 failed TOTP attempts, invalidate the `tmpToken` so the user must re-authenticate with their password before retrying.
3. Add a test that submits 6 incorrect TOTP codes in rapid succession and asserts the 6th returns HTTP 429.
Verification: Submit 6 wrong TOTP codes against `POST /rest/2fa/verify` with the same `tmpToken` within 1 minute and assert the 6th response is HTTP 429.
Reference: CWE-307

data.name: Web3 / Wallet / NFT Surface
data.description: Blockchain/web3 endpoints handling wallet addresses, NFT minting, and on-chain key material (ethers). Internet-facing crypto-asset surface with its own key-handling and ownership-verification trust boundary.

threats.title: [F-012] Hardcoded BIP-39 Mnemonic (routes/checkKeys.ts:10)
threats.description:
An attacker reads the public Juice Shop source repository and finds the twelve-word BIP-39 mnemonic `purpose betray marriage blame crunch monitor spin slide donate sport lift clutch` at `routes/checkKeys.ts:10`. Using ethers.js `HDNodeWallet.fromPhrase()` or any BIP-39-compatible tool, the attacker derives the wallet's private key, public key, and Ethereum address in under a second. Any funds, NFTs, or on-chain credentials held by that wallet are permanently accessible to the attacker — regardless of how the application-level challenge gate is configured. The mnemonic is evaluated on every request to `POST /rest/web3/submitKey`, so even if the route required authentication, the credential is already public through version control history.

Impact: Full compromise of the application-controlled Ethereum wallet — private key, public key, and Ethereum address are all derivable from the exposed mnemonic by any reader of the source.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-798
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`routes/checkKeys.ts:10` assigns the twelve-word mnemonic as a string literal; `HDNodeWallet.fromPhrase()` at line 11 derives a fully operable private key from it on every request.
- routes/checkKeys.ts:10

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-6 web3-nft → external (outbound): The assumption that blockchain RPC responses are validated before wallet state is accepted is moot: the application's own private key is already derivable from the source, so the boundary assumption provides no defence.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-012 (F-012)
threats.mitigation:
M-011 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Rotate the exposed mnemonic immediately: generate a new BIP-39 mnemonic, transfer any on-chain assets, and revoke the old wallet.
2. Store the replacement mnemonic or derived private key in a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) or in an environment variable (`WALLET_MNEMONIC`) loaded at startup — never in source.
3. Replace `const mnemonic = '...'` in `routes/checkKeys.ts:10` with `const mnemonic = process.env.WALLET_MNEMONIC` and add a startup guard that throws if the variable is absent.
4. Add a pre-commit hook or CI secret-scanning step (e.g. `git-secrets`, `truffleHog`) to block future mnemonic or private-key literals from reaching version control.
Verification: Confirm the mnemonic string is absent from all git history (`git log -S 'purpose betray' --all` returns no commits); verify the server refuses to start when `WALLET_MNEMONIC` is unset; confirm `GET /rest/web3/submitKey` returns 500 with a generic error when the env var is missing rather than exposing any key material.
Reference: CWE-798

threats.title: [F-017] Open Redirect Allowlist Bypass via Substring Match (routes/redirect.ts:16)
threats.description:
An attacker crafts a URL such as `https://evil.example.com/?q=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop` and sends it as the `?to=` parameter to `GET /redirect`. The allowlist check at `lib/insecurity.ts:136` uses `url.includes(allowedUrl)` — a substring match — so the attacker's URL passes because it contains the allowlisted GitHub URL as a query parameter. The server issues a `302` redirect to the attacker-controlled domain. The attacker distributes the crafted Juice Shop redirect link to users; when users click it, they land on a phishing page while the URL bar initially shows the trusted Juice Shop domain.

Impact: An attacker can host a phishing page on any domain and redirect Juice Shop users to it using the application's own trusted domain as the initial URL, increasing the credibility of credential-harvesting or malware campaigns.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-601
CVSS v4: 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:A/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`lib/insecurity.ts:136` uses `url.includes(allowedUrl)` instead of a prefix or exact match, making the substring of any allowlisted URL sufficient to pass the redirect gate.
- routes/redirect.ts:16

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-017 (F-017)
threats.mitigation:
M-016 — Validate redirect targets against an allowlist (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Replace `url.includes(allowedUrl)` with `utils.startsWith(url, allowedUrl)` in `lib/insecurity.ts:136` — `startsWith` is already imported and uses `str.indexOf(prefix) === 0` which enforces prefix matching.
2. Audit the allowlist entries to ensure all entries include the full path needed, and remove overly broad entries (bare domains without trailing slash).
3. Add a unit test asserting that `https://evil.com?q=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop` is rejected by `isRedirectAllowed`.
Verification: Send `GET /redirect?to=https://evil.example.com/?q=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop`; server must return HTTP 406. Send `GET /redirect?to=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop`; server must return HTTP 302.
Reference: CWE-601

threats.title: [F-028] Unvalidated Wallet Address in NFT Challenge Verification (routes/nftMint.ts:41)
threats.description:
An attacker POSTs `{"walletAddress": "<any string>"}` to `POST /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify`. The handler at `routes/nftMint.ts:41` reads `req.body.walletAddress` and checks whether it exists in the `addressesMinted` in-memory Set. No authentication, no wallet address format validation, and no ownership proof is required. If the attacker can predict or observe which addresses are in the Set (e.g., by monitoring the on-chain `NFTMinted` event for other users), they can submit that address to claim another user's NFT minting event and have the challenge marked as solved under their session. Additionally, submitting the correct address deletes it from the Set at line 43, denying the legitimate minter their challenge credit.

Impact: An attacker can claim NFT minting challenge credit for any wallet address in the server Set, and simultaneously deny the legitimate minter their credit by removing the address from the Set.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-862
CVSS v4: 8.7 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`routes/nftMint.ts:41` reads `req.body.walletAddress` and compares directly against `addressesMinted` with no caller identity binding, no authentication, and no Ethereum address format check.
- routes/nftMint.ts:41

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-028 (F-028)
threats.mitigation:
M-027 — Enforce server-side authorization on every endpoint (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Add `security.isAuthorized()` middleware to the `/rest/web3/walletNFTVerify` route in `server.ts` so that only authenticated users can call this endpoint.
2. Validate that `req.body.walletAddress` is a syntactically valid Ethereum address using `ethers.isAddress(req.body.walletAddress)` before checking the Set; return 400 on invalid format.
3. Store minted addresses mapped to authenticated user IDs (not just bare addresses) so that only the user whose JWT matches the wallet can claim the challenge.
Verification: Send POST with `walletAddress: 'not-an-address'`; expect HTTP 400. Send unauthenticated POST with a valid address; expect HTTP 401 after auth middleware is added.
Reference: CWE-862

threats.title: [F-048] Missing Authentication on Web3 Challenge Routes
threats.description:
An attacker sends unauthenticated HTTP requests to any of the five web3 endpoints registered in `server.ts` lines 641–645. None of these routes carry `security.isAuthorized()` middleware, unlike adjacent routes such as `/rest/products/reviews` at line 635. An attacker can POST arbitrary wallet addresses to `/rest/web3/walletNFTVerify` and `/rest/web3/walletExploitAddress`, register external wallet addresses into the server-side challenge state, and manipulate challenge completion records without holding a valid JWT session. An attacker who races the NFT event listener can also claim challenge-solved status for any wallet address.

Impact: Any unauthenticated caller can manipulate the NFT challenge state, register arbitrary wallet addresses in server memory, and claim challenge completion without owning the relevant wallet.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-306
CVSS v4: 8.7 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`server.ts:641-645` registers all five `/rest/web3/*` routes without `security.isAuthorized()` middleware; `routes/web3Wallet.ts:13` and `routes/nftMint.ts:38` contain no in-handler auth checks.
- routes/web3Wallet.ts:13

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → backend-api (internet-facing): The boundary assumption that every state-changing route is gated behind security.isAuthorized() expressJwt is violated: none of the five /rest/web3/* route registrations include that middleware.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-048 (F-048)
threats.mitigation:
M-047 — Require authentication on every exposed endpoint (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Wrap each state-changing web3 route in `server.ts` with `security.isAuthorized()` to enforce JWT authentication, matching the pattern already used on lines 603–635.
2. For `/rest/web3/submitKey`, also bind the submitted key comparison to `req.user.id` so challenge credit is awarded only to the authenticated user.
3. Apply rate limiting to all five routes using `express-rate-limit` to prevent bulk challenge-manipulation from authenticated or unauthenticated callers.
Verification: Send unauthenticated POST to `/rest/web3/walletNFTVerify`; server must return HTTP 401. Send the same request with a valid JWT; server must return a non-401 response.
Reference: CWE-306

threats.title: [F-063] Unbounded In-Memory Set Growth Without Rate Limiting
threats.description:
An attacker sends high-volume POST requests to `/rest/web3/walletExploitAddress` — which has no authentication or rate limiting. At `routes/web3Wallet.ts:16`, each request adds `req.body.walletAddress` to the module-global `walletsConnected` Set before the try block. Since Ethereum addresses are strings and differ per request (e.g., sequential hex strings), each request adds a new entry to the Set. Over time the Set grows unboundedly, consuming heap memory until the Node.js process is killed by the OS or crashes with OOM. The same pattern exists in `routes/nftMint.ts:10` (`addressesMinted`) but requires an on-chain event to populate, making it less directly exploitable.

Impact: An attacker can exhaust server heap memory by flooding `/rest/web3/walletExploitAddress` with distinct wallet addresses, crashing the Node.js process and taking down the application.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-400
CVSS v4: 8.7 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`routes/web3Wallet.ts:16` calls `walletsConnected.add(metamaskAddress)` unconditionally before any validation or rate check; the Set at line 10 has no capacity limit.
- routes/web3Wallet.ts:16

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-063 (F-063)
threats.mitigation:
M-062 — Rate-limit expensive requests and bound input size (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Apply `express-rate-limit` middleware to all `/rest/web3/*` routes, limiting each IP to a reasonable request rate (e.g., 10 requests per minute).
2. Add a maximum size guard before adding to `walletsConnected`: `if (walletsConnected.size < MAX_TRACKED_WALLETS) walletsConnected.add(metamaskAddress)` where `MAX_TRACKED_WALLETS` is a configurable constant (e.g., 10 000).
3. Move `walletsConnected.add(metamaskAddress)` to inside the `try` block, after validating that `metamaskAddress` is a valid Ethereum address via `ethers.isAddress()`.
Verification: Send 20 000 POST requests with distinct addresses to `/rest/web3/walletExploitAddress`; server heap usage must remain bounded and the endpoint must begin returning 429 after the rate limit is reached.
Reference: CWE-400
